INTRODUCTION

[1] Ms. XXXX, you are acting as the designated representative for your minor children. You are citizens of Angola. You stated that you were threatened by a political movement by reason of your link to your father, who was an influential member of a political party in your country. You also stated that you were sexually assaulted by criminals in March 2019.1

[2] The Minister of Public Safety (the Minister) intervened in your refugee protection claims, submitted that they lacked credibility and asked the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) to reject them.2

[3] The RPD rejected your refugee protection claims after finding that you were not credible.3

[4] On appeal, you presented evidence, requested that an oral hearing be held and submitted that the RPD erred in its assessment of your credibility.4

[5] After analyzing your record, I conclude that the documentary evidence presented on appeal is not admissible and that it is not possible to hold a hearing. I also conclude that the RPD did not err as you allege.

[6] In light of these conclusions, your appeal is dismissed.
I. EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL

[7] The Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules) provide that the person who is the subject of the appeal must submit a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding how the documentary evidence they wish to cite on appeal meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and how that evidence relates to them.5

[8] In your written statement, you submit that you presented evidence referred to in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA,6 namely, testimony from your father's brother-in-law.7

[9] In your memorandum, you submit that this evidence meets the requirements in subsection 110(4) because it was obtained after the RPD hearing and, at the time of that hearing, you could not have obtained it because you had had no contact with the person who provided the written testimony. You also submit that this evidence relates to you, because it brings to light the threats and the assault you suffered in Angola.8

[10] I consider it necessary to remember that subsection 110(3) of the IRPA expressly provides that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) must generally proceed without an oral hearing, on the basis of the RPD record.

[11] The testimony from your father's step-brother, dated September 3, 2020, confirms that your father had been a politician and senior member of a major political party forming the opposition in your country and that he had experienced several problems during his life.
[12] In my opinion, this written testimony relates to events that arose before the RPD rejected your refugee protection claims.

[10] I consider it necessary to remember that subsection 110(3) of the IRPA expressly provides that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) must generally proceed without an oral hearing, on the basis of the RPD record. Subsection 110(4) provides an exception to this general rule. The existence of criteria governing the admissibility of new evidence on appeal helps to preserve the integrity of the judicial process by promoting finality with respect to the factual record at the first level of decision-making, with limited exceptions, and encouraging the narrowing of issues as matters move up the appellate ladder.9

[11] The testimony from your father's step-brother, dated September 3, 2020, confirms that your father had been a politician and senior member of a major political party forming the opposition in your country and that he had experienced several problems during his life. It states that your father's family was not spared from the threats hanging over him and that you had chosen to leave your country for your safety and to protect your life and your children's lives.

[12] In my opinion, this written testimony relates to events that arose before the RPD rejected your refugee protection claims. Furthermore, there are no statements in the written testimony that establish why it was not reasonably available or why you could not reasonably have been expected to have presented it to the RPD before it rejected your refugee protection claims. As a result, I have reached the conclusion that this testimony aims primarily to confirm events or allegations that have been analyzed by the RPD and that there is no cause to accept it as evidence on appeal.
II. ORAL HEARING BEFORE THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

[13] The RAD Rules provide that the person who is the subject of the appeal must provide a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding why the RAD should hold an oral hearing.10

[14] In your memorandum, you submit that the evidence you presented on appeal shows that your testimony is credible with regard to the threats and the rape you suffered and with respect to what your father experienced during his lifetime.11

You also submit that this evidence relates to you, because it brings to light the threats and the assault you suffered in Angola.8

[10] I consider it necessary to remember that subsection 110(3) of the IRPA expressly provides that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) must generally proceed without an oral hearing, on the basis of the RPD record. Subsection 110(4) provides an exception to this general rule. The existence of criteria governing the admissibility of new evidence on appeal helps to preserve the integrity of the judicial process by promoting finality with respect to the factual record at the first level of decision-making, with limited exceptions, and encouraging the narrowing of issues as matters move up the appellate ladder.9

[11] The testimony from your father's step-brother, dated September 3, 2020, confirms that your father had been a politician and senior member of a major political party forming the opposition in your country and that he had experienced several problems during his life. It states that your father's family was not spared from the threats hanging over him and that you had chosen to leave your country for your safety and to protect your life and your children's lives.

[12] In my opinion, this written testimony relates to events that arose before the RPD rejected your refugee protection claims. II. ORAL HEARING BEFORE THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION

[13] The RAD Rules provide that the person who is the subject of the appeal must provide a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding why the RAD should hold an oral hearing.10

[14] In your memorandum, you submit that the evidence you presented on appeal shows that your testimony is credible with regard to the threats and the rape you suffered and with respect to what your father experienced during his lifetime.11

[15] The onus rests with the RAD to determine whether the criteria set out in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA have been met.12 One of the criteria in this subsection is that evidence presented on appeal must be found admissible. However, I found that the evidence you presented on appeal was not admissible. Therefore, it is not possible to hold an oral hearing.13

III. ANALYSIS OF THE APPEAL

[16] The RAD's role is not to conduct a de novo consideration of a claim for refugee protection but rather to determine whether the RPD erred as submitted.14 I have conducted my own analysis of your record, primarily by reading the transcript of the RPD hearing15 and reviewing the documentary evidence. In my opinion, the correctness standard of review must be applied.16
A. The Refugee Protection Division's alleged errors

[17] The RAD Rules provide that the person who is the subject of the appeal must identify i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal and ii) where the errors are located in the RPD's decision or in the transcript or in any other recording of the hearing.17

[18] When asked to explain the errors that are the grounds of the appeal and to provide full and detailed submissions concerning each error, your counsel wrote the following on this topic:
[Translation]
The panel draws a negative inference regarding the appellant's testimony about her relationship with her husband. The appellant did testify during the hearing that she has no contact with her husband due to the suffering he inflicted upon her. She has never looked for him and does not know where he is. It is possible that her brothers are friends with her husband on Facebook; however, does that mean that the appellant has information about her husband?
The panel rejects the appellant's explanations with regard to her professional background and considers that they undermine the appellant's credibility. However, the appellant testified that she has worked at a pharmacy, that she is a reverend and that she had a hair salon. She states that she is a reverend in her visa application, which is not surprising because she applied for a United States visa on that basis. She had a salon but no longer works there. Was she required to declare that as work?
The panel rejects the appellant's explanation that she was unaware that she had to provide the address where she had lived in the U.S. She gave testimony on that topic, stating that she was unaware that she had to provide that address. That is understandable considering that she had thought that she could only provide home addresses and not temporary addresses, such as the one in the U.S.
The panel draws a negative inference from the appellant's failure to mention that she had been attacked by members of the military. It is true that she did not talk about military members; however, in her written account, she makes reference to criminals who raped her and states that she lost consciousness. What is certain is that she was threatened and raped.18
B. According to my own analysis, the Refugee Protection Division did not err as you allege

[19] After conducting my own analysis of your record, I have concluded that the RPD did not err as you seem to allege. The reasons are as follows.

[20] In its decision, the RPD concluded that the cumulative contradictions and omissions it identified undermined your overall credibility.19 These contradictions and omissions concern:
- Your testimony that you have been unaware of your husband's whereabouts for seven years already even though you applied for a U.S. visa with him in October 2015 and your explanation for this contradiction, namely, that your husband had made you suffer a lot and that you have memory problems and problems with dates;20
- The pages from a social network showing that your husband worked in Angola in 2019 and that he was friends with people that appear to be your brothers. This information contradicts your testimony that your husband had disappeared. Afterwards, you continued to state that he had disappeared and explained that you had no information and had made no effort to find him;21
- Your failure to state in your IMM 5669 form that you had a hair salon and that you work as a XXXX in a church;22
- Your failure to state in the same form that you had had lengthy stays in the U.S. and that the U.S. authorities had refused to issue you a visa23 on several occasions;
- Your failure to state in your BOC Form that, on more than six occasions, armed individuals had come to your home to threaten you. You explained this omission by stating that you had wanted to elaborate on this during the hearing and that you had always been threatened;24 and
- Your failure to state in your BOC Form that members of the military had come to your home in March 2019 and had wanted to kill you, as they had killed your father. You explained this omission by stating that you had not provided the details in your written account.25

[21] When claimants swear to the truth of certain allegations, they are presumed to tell the truth. However, this presumption is rebuttable where the evidence is inconsistent with the testimony or where the RPD is unsatisfied with the explanation for those inconsistencies.26 The RPD may make adverse findings based on implausibility, inconsistencies or omissions. It is the entirety of the evidence that must be assessed.27

[22] After analyzing your record, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err when it explained the various contradictions and omissions that undermined your overall credibility. With all due respect, the arguments your counsel presented on appeal do not lead to the conclusion that the RPD erred when it rejected your refugee protection claims.

[23] Furthermore, in its decision, the RPD analyzed the medical certificate you filed in evidence.28 It concluded that it does not confirm that you were sexually assaulted by members of a political party in your country or by members of the military. The RPD found that this evidence was based on your testimony, which was not credible, and that it was insufficient to overcome your credibility issues.29

[24] Documentary evidence is not assessed in isolation from the overall refugee protection claim. As the RPD found that you were not credible, it was able to have credibility concerns with the documentary evidence presented in support of your refugee protection claim.30 The weight of evidence is the persuasiveness of some evidence in relation to other evidence.31 According to my own analysis of the record, the RPD did not err when it gave no weight or probative value to the medical certificate or when it explained why.

[19] After conducting my own analysis of your record, I have concluded that the RPD did not err as you seem to allege. The reasons are as follows.

[20] In its decision, the RPD concluded that the cumulative contradictions and omissions it identified undermined your overall credibility.19 These contradictions and omissions concern:
- Your testimony that you have been unaware of your husband's whereabouts for seven years already even though you applied for a U.S. visa with him in October 2015 and your explanation for this contradiction, namely, that your husband had made you suffer a lot and that you have memory problems and problems with dates;20
- The pages from a social network showing that your husband worked in Angola in 2019 and that he was friends with people that appear to be your brothers. This information contradicts your testimony that your husband had disappeared. Afterwards, you continued to state that he had disappeared and explained that you had no information and had made no effort to find him;21
- Your failure to state in your IMM 5669 form that you had a hair salon and that you work as a XXXX in a church;22
- Your failure to state in the same form that you had had lengthy stays in the U.S. and that the U.S. authorities had refused to issue you a visa23 on several occasions;
- Your failure to state in your BOC Form that, on more than six occasions, armed individuals had come to your home to threaten you. You explained this omission by stating that you had wanted to elaborate on this during the hearing and that you had always been threatened;24 and

It is the entirety of the evidence that must be assessed.27

With all due respect, the arguments your counsel presented on appeal do not lead to the conclusion that the RPD erred when it rejected your refugee protection claims.

[23] Furthermore, in its decision, the RPD analyzed the medical certificate you filed in evidence.28 It concluded that it does not confirm that you were sexually assaulted by members of a political party in your country or by members of the military. The RPD found that this evidence was based on your testimony, which was not credible, and that it was insufficient to overcome your credibility issues.29

[24] Documentary evidence is not assessed in isolation from the overall refugee protection claim. As the RPD found that you were not credible, it was able to have credibility concerns with the documentary evidence presented in support of your refugee protection claim.30 The weight of evidence is the persuasiveness of some evidence in relation to other evidence.31 According to my own analysis of the record, the RPD did not err when it gave no weight or probative value to the medical certificate or when it explained why.

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] Ms. XXXX, you are acting as the designated representative for your minor children. You are citizens of Angola. You stated that you were threatened by a political movement by reason of your link to your father, who was an influential member of a political party in your country. You also stated that you were sexually assaulted by criminals in March 2019.1
[2] The Minister of Public Safety (the Minister) intervened in your refugee protection claims, submitted that they lacked credibility and asked the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) to reject them.2
[3] The RPD rejected your refugee protection claims after finding that you were not credible.3
[4] On appeal, you presented evidence, requested that an oral hearing be held and submitted that the RPD erred in its assessment of your credibility.4

[5] After analyzing your record, I conclude that the documentary evidence presented on appeal is not admissible and that it is not possible to hold a hearing. I also conclude that the RPD did not err as you allege.

[6] In light of these conclusions, your appeal is dismissed.
I. EVIDENCE PRESENTED ON APPEAL

[7] The Refugee Appeal Division Rules (RAD Rules) provide that the person who is the subject of the appeal must submit a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding how the documentary evidence they wish to cite on appeal meets the requirements of subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and how that evidence relates to them.5
[8] In your written statement, you submit that you presented evidence referred to in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA,6 namely, testimony from your father's brother-in-law.7

[9] In your memorandum, you submit that this evidence meets the requirements in subsection 110(4) because it was obtained after the RPD hearing and, at the time of that hearing, you could not have obtained it because you had had no contact with the person who provided the written testimony. You also submit that this evidence relates to you, because it brings to light the threats and the assault you suffered in Angola.8

[10] I consider it necessary to remember that subsection 110(3) of the IRPA expressly provides that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) must generally proceed without an oral hearing, on the basis of the RPD record. Subsection 110(4) provides an exception to this general rule. The existence of criteria governing the admissibility of new evidence on appeal helps to preserve the integrity of the judicial process by promoting finality with respect to the factual record at the first level of decision-making, with limited exceptions, and encouraging the narrowing of issues as matters move up the appellate ladder.9

[11] The testimony from your father's step-brother, dated September 3, 2020, confirms that your father had been a politician and senior member of a major political party forming the opposition in your country and that he had experienced several problems during his life. It states that your father's family was not spared from the threats hanging over him and that you had chosen to leave your country for your safety and to protect your life and your children's lives.

[12] In my opinion, this written testimony relates to events that arose before the RPD rejected your refugee protection claims. Furthermore, there are no statements in the written testimony that establish why it was not reasonably available or why you could not reasonably have been expected to have presented it to the RPD before it rejected your refugee protection claims. As a result, I have reached the conclusion that this testimony aims primarily to confirm events or allegations that have been analyzed by the RPD and that there is no cause to accept it as evidence on appeal.
II. ORAL HEARING BEFORE THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION
[13] The RAD Rules provide that the person who is the subject of the appeal must provide a memorandum that includes full and detailed submissions regarding why the RAD should hold an oral hearing.10

[14] In your memorandum, you submit that the evidence you presented on appeal shows that your testimony is credible with regard to the threats and the rape you suffered and with respect to what your father experienced during his lifetime.11

[15] The onus rests with the RAD to determine whether the criteria set out in subsection 110(6) of the IRPA have been met.12 One of the criteria in this subsection is that evidence presented on appeal must be found admissible. However, I found that the evidence you presented on appeal was not admissible. Therefore, it is not possible to hold an oral hearing.13
III. ANALYSIS OF THE APPEAL

[16] The RAD's role is not to conduct a de novo consideration of a claim for refugee protection but rather to determine whether the RPD erred as submitted.14 I have conducted my own analysis of your record, primarily by reading the transcript of the RPD hearing15 and reviewing the documentary evidence. In my opinion, the correctness standard of review must be applied.16
A. The Refugee Protection Division's alleged errors

[17] The RAD Rules provide that the person who is the subject of the appeal must identify i) the errors that are the grounds of the appeal and ii) where the errors are located in the RPD's decision or in the transcript or in any other recording of the hearing.17

[18] When asked to explain the errors that are the grounds of the appeal and to provide full and detailed submissions concerning each error, your counsel wrote the following on this topic:
[Translation]
The panel draws a negative inference regarding the appellant's testimony about her relationship with her husband. The appellant did testify during the hearing that she has no contact with her husband due to the suffering he inflicted upon her. She has never looked for him and does not know where he is. It is possible that her brothers are friends with her husband on Facebook; however, does that mean that the appellant has information about her husband?
The panel rejects the appellant's explanations with regard to her professional background and considers that they undermine the appellant's credibility. However, the appellant testified that she has worked at a pharmacy, that she is a reverend and that she had a hair salon. She states that she is a reverend in her visa application, which is not surprising because she applied for a United States visa on that basis. She had a salon but no longer works there. Was she required to declare that as work?
The panel rejects the appellant's explanation that she was unaware that she had to provide the address where she had lived in the U.S. She gave testimony on that topic, stating that she was unaware that she had to provide that address. That is understandable considering that she had thought that she could only provide home addresses and not temporary addresses, such as the one in the U.S.
The panel draws a negative inference from the appellant's failure to mention that she had been attacked by members of the military. It is true that she did not talk about military members; however, in her written account, she makes reference to criminals who raped her and states that she lost consciousness. What is certain is that she was threatened and raped.18
B. According to my own analysis, the Refugee Protection Division did not err as you allege
[19] After conducting my own analysis of your record, I have concluded that the RPD did not err as you seem to allege. The reasons are as follows.

[20] In its decision, the RPD concluded that the cumulative contradictions and omissions it identified undermined your overall credibility.19 These contradictions and omissions concern:
- Your testimony that you have been unaware of your husband's whereabouts for seven years already even though you applied for a U.S. visa with him in October 2015 and your explanation for this contradiction, namely, that your husband had made you suffer a lot and that you have memory problems and problems with dates;20
- The pages from a social network showing that your husband worked in Angola in 2019 and that he was friends with people that appear to be your brothers. This information contradicts your testimony that your husband had disappeared. Afterwards, you continued to state that he had disappeared and explained that you had no information and had made no effort to find him;21
- Your failure to state in your IMM 5669 form that you had a hair salon and that you work as a XXXX in a church;22
- Your failure to state in the same form that you had had lengthy stays in the U.S. and that the U.S. authorities had refused to issue you a visa23 on several occasions;
- Your failure to state in your BOC Form that, on more than six occasions, armed individuals had come to your home to threaten you. You explained this omission by stating that you had wanted to elaborate on this during the hearing and that you had always been threatened;24 and
- Your failure to state in your BOC Form that members of the military had come to your home in March 2019 and had wanted to kill you, as they had killed your father. You explained this omission by stating that you had not provided the details in your written account.25

[21] When claimants swear to the truth of certain allegations, they are presumed to tell the truth. However, this presumption is rebuttable where the evidence is inconsistent with the testimony or where the RPD is unsatisfied with the explanation for those inconsistencies.26 The RPD may make adverse findings based on implausibility, inconsistencies or omissions. It is the entirety of the evidence that must be assessed.27

[22] After analyzing your record, I am of the opinion that the RPD did not err when it explained the various contradictions and omissions that undermined your overall credibility. With all due respect, the arguments your counsel presented on appeal do not lead to the conclusion that the RPD erred when it rejected your refugee protection claims.

[23] Furthermore, in its decision, the RPD analyzed the medical certificate you filed in evidence.28 It concluded that it does not confirm that you were sexually assaulted by members of a political party in your country or by members of the military. The RPD found that this evidence was based on your testimony, which was not credible, and that it was insufficient to overcome your credibility issues.29

[24] Documentary evidence is not assessed in isolation from the overall refugee protection claim. As the RPD found that you were not credible, it was able to have credibility concerns with the documentary evidence presented in support of your refugee protection claim.30 The weight of evidence is the persuasiveness of some evidence in relation to other evidence.31 According to my own analysis of the record, the RPD did not err when it gave no weight or probative value to the medical certificate or when it explained why.
CONCLUSION

[25] For these reasons, I confirm the determination of the RPD, namely, that you and your minor children have failed to establish that you have a well-founded fear of persecution within the meaning of section 96 or that you would be subject to a risk referred to in section 97 of the IRPA if you had to return to Angola.

[26] Your appeal is dismissed.
(signed)
Alain Bissonnette
Me Alain Bissonnette
February 8, 2021
